please / here you go / you’re welcome

Proszę is Polish’s most important A1 politeness marker. It means please (with a request), here you go (handing something over), you’re welcome (after dziękuję), and even pardon? (asking to repeat). With an infinitive (proszę powtórzyć) it builds polite requests. Note: poproszę is the perfective form of the same root and is the natural ordering marker in service contexts.

Dworzec is the A1 standard word for train station (usually rail; a bus station is dworzec autobusowy). It’s a masculine inanimate noun; plural dworce. In Gdzie jest dworzec? it stands in the nominative as the subject of jest. Note: stacja is more general (radio station, metro station, gas station) — for a railway terminal, prefer dworzec.

Kawa is feminine. In Poproszę kawę the noun is in the accusative singular (kawę) because it’s the direct object of the polite request. Plural: kawy. For two coffees: Poproszę dwie kawy. Poproszę is the perfective form of prosić — in service contexts almost always the right choice because each request is a single, completed action.

Ile is the A1 standard question word for amounts and prices — invariant and usually at the start of the sentence. Works for both countable and uncountable things. Other A1 question words for context: co (what), gdzie (where), kto (who), kiedy (when), jak (how), dlaczego (why). Note: ile itself never changes form, but the counted noun goes in the genitive (e.g., ile kawy — how much coffee).

Pociąg is the A1 standard word for a railway train. It’s a masculine inanimate noun; plural pociągi. In O której odjeżdża pociąg? it stands in the nominative as the subject of odjeżdża; the verb is imperfective because schedules describe recurring events. No false friends in English — pociąg just means train.

Pomoc is feminine (nominative: pomoc, genitive: pomocy). Important: the verb potrzebować (to need) takes the GENITIVE — Potrzebuję pomocy is literally "I need of-the-help". Same pattern: potrzebuję wody (I need water), potrzebuję czasu (I need time). This is a core A1 case rule with no direct equivalent in English; think of it as Polish marking the noun’s role with a different ending (similar to how English shifts who → whom).

Bardzo (very / really) is Polish’s main A1 intensity adverb. It modifies verbs (bardzo lubię — I really like), adjectives (bardzo dobry — very good), and adverbs (bardzo dobrze — very well). With the impersonal podobać się construction (something is pleasing to someone), it builds the natural "I really like it here". Note: Polish keeps lubić (someone likes something — transitive) and podobać się (something is pleasing to someone — impersonal) more clearly apart than English does.
Warm cafe interior, a short positive small-talk comment.

Jutro (tomorrow) sits alongside dzisiaj (today) and wczoraj (yesterday) as a core A1 time anchor. Watch out: in the set farewell Do jutra! the word is in the genitive (jutra), because the preposition do takes the genitive case. Same pattern: Do zobaczenia! (See you — literally "until the seeing"), Do widzenia! In the sentence itself (as a plain adverb), jutro stays unchanged: Spotykamy się jutro (we meet tomorrow).
Warm late-day light, a short friendly meet-up confirmation.
Close the encounter with thanks and a polite formal goodbye.

End of the day at the counter, a warm thank-you and a polite goodbye.

Do widzenia is the canonical formal farewell — literally "until the seeing" (do + genitive of widzenie). It fits service contexts, strangers, and business situations. More casual options: cześć (also works as hello!), na razie (for now / bye for now), do zobaczenia (see you soon). Time-of-day variants: dobry wieczór (good evening) as a greeting, dobranoc (good night) as a farewell before sleep.
Warm farewell at the counter, gentle daylight.

Pytanie is neuter (nominative and accusative are identical: pytanie). Plural: pytania. In Mam pytanie it stands in the accusative as the direct object of mam (from mieć — to have). An open A1 help-ask in Polish typically opens with mam pytanie before the actual question comes.

Napisać is the perfective form of the verb pair pisać/napisać (to write). Perfective means one-time, completed — perfect for a single concrete request. With Proszę + perfective infinitive you build a polite request for one specific, finished action. For a habit or process you’d use the imperfective pisać instead (e.g., lubię pisać — I like writing).
Counter, a notepad, a calm write-it-down request.

Mapa is feminine. Nominative singular: mapa. Locative singular: mapie. After the preposition na (for a flat surface), the noun goes into the locative — hence na mapie (on the map). Same pattern: na ulicy (on the street), na stole (on the table). Plural nominative: mapy.

Tamto is the neuter demonstrative for a distant object — "that one over there". It matches the gender of the noun it refers to: masculine tamten, feminine tamta, neuter tamto. The near counterpart is to (this). Polish makes the to / tamto contrast available much more cleanly than English, which often blurs "this one" and "that one" in casual speech.

Jeszcze is a core A1 adverb with two main meanings: "still" for remaining stock (czy jest jeszcze chleb? — is there still bread?) and "still / yet" for an ongoing state (jeszcze tu jestem — I’m still here). In availability questions it’s the standard marker — neater than the English "any X left?" pattern.
Shop counter, one of the last loaves of bread, a calm question about what’s left.

Karta is feminine. Nominative singular: karta. Accusative singular: kartę. But in Czy mogę zapłacić kartą? the noun is in the INSTRUMENTAL singular (kartą), because płacić / zapłacić takes the instrumental for the means — "with what / how do I pay". Same pattern: gotówką (with cash), kartą kredytową (with a credit card). Plural: karty.

Paragon is masculine inanimate. Nominative and accusative singular are identical: paragon — so Poproszę paragon takes no ending change. Plural: paragony. Note: paragon here means the printed cash receipt (relevant for tax purposes); an official business invoice is faktura, and rachunek is more typically the bill in a restaurant.

Rezerwacja is feminine. Nominative singular: rezerwacja. Accusative singular: rezerwację (-a → -ę). In Mam rezerwację the noun stands in the accusative as the direct object of mam. The set front-desk phrase na nazwisko (under the name) uses na + accusative; nazwisko is neuter (accusative and nominative are the same). Plural nominative: rezerwacje.

Dobrze is the adverb of dobry (good). Polish adverbs are invariant — they never change form. In check questions, Czy to dobrze? means "is that right?". As a reply, tak, dobrze (yes, ok) signals agreement. The opposite is źle (wrong / badly). Note: the adjective dobry changes by gender (dobry / dobra / dobre); the adverb dobrze always stays the same.

Chwila is feminine. Nominative singular: chwila. In service Polish, the diminutive chwilka / chwileczka is used far more often — it sounds softer and more polite than the plain chwila. In Chwileczkę, proszę it stands in the accusative (chwileczkę), because an implied "wait / give me a moment" hangs in the air behind the noun. Synonyms: moment (a loanword), sekunda (second). Plural: chwile.
Counter, a friendly brief pause, a soft wait request.

Lewo is a neuter direction noun, used in the fixed phrase w lewo (to the left) where w plus the accusative shows motion towards a direction. Its pair is w prawo (to the right); other A1 directions are prosto (straight ahead) and w tył (backward). Note that prawo on its own also means "law / right" (the legal sense), but the meaning is clear from context.

Daleko is an invariant A1 adverb of distance — it never changes for gender or number, just like English "far". Its pair is blisko (near). Useful A1 expansions: jak daleko? (how far?), niedaleko (not far), gdzieś daleko (somewhere far away). Note that Polish uses czy as a yes/no question particle at the start of a sentence; English uses subject-verb word order instead.

Otwarte is the neuter form of the adjective otwarty (open). Polish adjectives change for gender, so you use otwarty with a masculine noun (sklep otwarty — the shop is open), otwarta with a feminine noun (apteka otwarta — the pharmacy is open), and otwarte with a neuter noun or a general "it". Its pair is zamknięte (closed); shop windows often show czynne (in service) with the same meaning.

Autobus is a masculine inanimate noun; its plural is autobusy. Here it is in the nominative as the subject of jedzie (the 3rd-person singular form of jechać, the imperfective verb for "to go by vehicle"). The preposition do (to) takes the genitive — similar to how English "to" takes the basic noun form — but centrum is a borrowed neuter noun that never changes its ending. Other A1 transit nouns: tramwaj (tram), metro (subway, also invariable).

Przystanek is a masculine inanimate noun; plural przystanki. In Czy to mój przystanek? it sits in the nominative as the predicate after to (this/it is). Unlike English "my", the Polish possessive changes to match its noun: mój with masculine nouns like przystanek, moja with a feminine noun such as stacja (moja stacja — my station), moje with neuter. English speakers have no equivalent — gender agreement is purely Polish.
On the bus, a calm confirmation just before getting off.

Bilet is a masculine inanimate noun, so its accusative singular looks identical to its nominative (bilet). Polish uses the accusative for direct objects, like English "I would like a ticket". The number jeden (one) also takes a masculine inanimate accusative form here to agree with bilet. For two of them you switch to the plural: Poproszę dwa bilety. Poproszę itself is the fixed "I would like / could I have" formula at counters.

Kiedy is the basic A1 question word for time (when) and never changes form. For clock times the question is o której (at what time). Zamykacie is the 2nd-person plural form of the imperfective verb zamykać (to close, as a habit such as opening hours). Polish often addresses shop staff collectively in this 2nd-person plural — closer to English "you" in "When do you close?" than to a formal singular.

Róg is a masculine inanimate noun; the basic (nominative) form is róg (with ó), and the locative singular is rogu. After na meaning "at a location/landmark", Polish uses the locative case, so the corner becomes na rogu (at the corner). English has no equivalent — we just say "at the corner" without changing the noun. Watch out: róg also means "horn" (animal or musical instrument), but the meaning is clear from context.
Street corner, a clear point to turn.

Taksówka is a feminine noun: nominative taksówka, instrumental taksówką. To say "by some means of transport" Polish puts the vehicle in the instrumental case — taksówką literally means "by/with a taxi". The same pattern gives autobusem (by bus), tramwajem (by tram), rowerem (by bike). The adverb pieszo (on foot) is invariant and works like English "on foot". English does not change the noun ending — it relies on the preposition "by".

Teraz is the A1 time anchor for "right now" and never changes form — no case or gender to worry about. Useful pairings: później (later), wkrótce (soon), zaraz (in a moment / right away). In this lesson przepraszam works as the apology sense ("sorry"), not as "excuse me" — you are softening a small mishap before asking what to do.

Stolik is the diminutive of stół (table) — masculine inanimate, and the standard restaurant word for a guest table. Polish marks roles with case endings rather than word order: dla (for) takes the genitive, so two people becomes dwóch osób (genitive plural). For a single guest you say dla jednej osoby (genitive singular feminine).

Menu is a French loanword: in Polish it is neuter and completely indeclinable, so the form never changes for case. The native Polish word is jadłospis (masculine), but modern restaurants prefer menu and it is fully A1-accepted. Czy at the start of the sentence is a yes/no question particle — English does the same job with the auxiliary "could".

Herbata is feminine, and the ending -a changes to -ę in the accusative (herbatę) when it is the direct object of poproszę. To add a side, Polish uses z (with) plus the instrumental case — a separate case English does not mark: z cytryną (lemon), z mlekiem (milk), z cukrem (sugar). Think of it as a built-in "with" tag attached to the noun ending.

Cukier is masculine inanimate. The dictionary form is cukier, but the e drops out in the genitive: cukru. The preposition bez (without) always takes the genitive — similar to how English "of" pulls a different form in "a cup of tea". So you say bez cukru, bez mleka (no milk), bez soli (no salt).

Świeży is the dictionary form of the adjective (masculine). Unlike English "fresh", which never changes, Polish adjectives must match the noun gender: świeży chleb (fresh bread, masculine), świeża bułka (fresh roll, feminine), świeże pieczywo (fresh baked goods, neuter). In a general question about an unspecified item, Czy to świeże? uses the neuter form as the default.
Bakery counter, a checking look, a freshness query.

Wszystko is a neuter indefinite pronoun for "everything (things)"; in this role its nominative and accusative forms are the same, so you do not change it here. Its counterparts are nic (nothing) and coś (something); for "everyone (people)" Polish uses wszyscy (masculine plural). To wszystko literally means "that's everything" and is the standard polite way to close an order.

Wynos is masculine inanimate. In the fixed phrase na wynos (to take away), the preposition na takes the accusative to mark a purpose. The opposite is na miejscu (to have here / eat in), which uses the locative case (miejsce → miejscu). Both phrases are A1 standard at Polish cafés and small restaurants.

Smaczne is the neuter form of smaczny (tasty). Polish adjectives must match the gender of the noun: smaczny obiad (a tasty lunch, masculine), smaczna zupa (a tasty soup, feminine), smaczne ciasto (a tasty cake, neuter). For a general "it was tasty" with no specific noun, Polish chooses the neuter as the default. Useful swaps: dobre (good), pyszne (delicious).

Pogoda is feminine — Polish assigns it a grammatical gender, even though English "weather" has none. That gender drives the adjective ending: ładna pogoda (nice weather, feminine -a), not ładny or ładne. Useful swaps: piękna pogoda (lovely weather), brzydka pogoda (bad weather).

Rachunek is masculine inanimate (plural rachunki), with the accusative form the same as the nominative. Three Polish words split what English mostly calls "bill" or "receipt": rachunek is the restaurant bill, paragon is the till slip you get when paying at a shop, and faktura is a formal business invoice. At a restaurant you almost always ask for the rachunek.

Jak is the A1 question word for manner — closest to English "how", though here it lines up with "what". It never changes form. The fixed expression Jak masz na imię? literally reads "how do you have for a name?" and is the casual-you way to ask a first name. The polite form swaps in pan (sir) or pani (madam): Jak pan / pani ma na imię? Answer with Mam na imię Anna (My name is Anna) or Nazywam się Kowalski (My surname is Kowalski).

Miło is the adverb form of the adjective miły (nice, kind). Polish adverbs never change form. The set reply Miło mi literally reads "[it is] pleasant to me" — the adverb pairs with the dative pronoun mi (to whom? to me). If the other person says it first, you can reply Mnie też (me too) or Cieszę się (I am glad). This is the universal A1 response after any introduction, formal or casual.

Skąd is the A1 question word for direction-of-origin — "from where". It never changes form. The answer uses z plus the genitive: z Polski (from Poland), z Niemiec (from Germany). Polish keeps three direction questions clearly separate: skąd (from where? — origin), gdzie (where? — location), dokąd (to where? — destination). Mixing them up is a common beginner slip: gdzie jesteś? asks where you currently are, while skąd jesteś? asks where you originally come from.

Stąd means "from here" — it points back to the current spot as the place someone comes from. Its partner is stamtąd ("from there"). Keep two ideas apart: stąd / stamtąd are about origin (from where), while tu / tutaj just mean "here" as a static location. Easy mix-up: skąd is the question word ("from where?") and stąd is the answer ("from here") — same root, different jobs. The opening Czy is a yes/no marker that English handles by inverting "are you", so it can stay untranslated.
A casual chat, a friendly question about where someone lives.

Czas is masculine inanimate, so the accusative form (when it is the direct object of masz / mieć — to have) is identical to the basic form. The plural czasy ("times / eras") is uncommon in everyday talk. Polish often uses a bare case form where English uses a preposition: wieczorem ("in the evening") is the instrumental of wieczór with no preposition. Other handy A1 time anchors: w weekend (on the weekend), dzisiaj (today), jutro (tomorrow).

Spotkać is the perfective half of the verb pair spotykać / spotkać (to meet). Adding the reflexive particle się turns it into spotkać się ("to meet each other"). The first-person-plural imperative spotkajmy się is the natural way to say "let's meet". To name the place, Polish uses w / na plus the locative case — the case for static "where": w kawiarni (at the café, locative of kawiarnia), w parku (in the park), na rynku (on the market square). A lighter alternative is Zobaczymy się w kawiarni ("see you at the café").

Może does two jobs at A1, and the context tells you which: (1) as a modal particle meaning "maybe / perhaps", as in Może jutro? ("Maybe tomorrow?"); (2) as the third-person-singular present of móc (to be able), as in Może pan pomóc? ("Could you help, sir?"). As a softener for postponing plans, może is the most natural A1 choice — polite, tentative, and easy to follow with a time word like jutro (tomorrow) or wkrótce (soon).

Cześć has a handy dual-use at A1: it works as both "hi" on arrival and "bye" on leaving, but only in the casual register. Use it with people you would call by first name — friends, classmates, peers. In service settings or with strangers, the formal pair stays standard: dzień dobry (good day / hello) and do widzenia (goodbye). Other informal goodbyes worth knowing: na razie (see you later), do zobaczenia (see you), and pa (very informal, often on the phone). Do jutra literally reads "until tomorrow" — do takes the genitive, so jutro becomes jutra.

Źle is the adverb form of the adjective zły (bad). Polish describes how you feel with the reflexive verb czuć się ("to feel oneself") plus an adverb, not an adjective: czuję się źle (I feel bad), czuję się dobrze (I feel good). The comparative pair is gorzej (worse) and lepiej (better). Note the gender trap: the adjective zły shifts ending by gender (zły / zła / złe), but the adverb źle never changes — same form for everyone.

Apteka is a feminine noun. The base (nominative) form is apteka — what is the pharmacy? — and after the preposition w ("in / at"), it shifts to the locative form aptece, so "at the pharmacy" is w aptece. In Czy tu jest apteka? the word stays in the nominative because it is the subject of jest ("is"). The plural is apteki. A true cognate of English "apothecary" but it just means a normal pharmacy / drugstore, marked in Poland by a green cross or a red Apteka sign.

Lekarstwo is a neuter noun, so its accusative (what do you want?) looks the same as its nominative — no ending change here. The plural is lekarstwa. Related A1 words: lek (medicine, masculine, shorter), tabletki (tablets, a true cognate with English "tablets"), recepta (prescription — a false friend: it does NOT mean "recipe", which is przepis). Lekarstwo is the broadest term and opens the conversation before specifics.

Boli is the 3rd person singular present of the imperfective verb boleć (to hurt). The Polish pain construction is upside-down from English: the body part is the subject (in the nominative — "who is hurting?" — głowa), and the person feeling the pain goes in the accusative (whom is it hurting? — mnie). So Boli mnie głowa literally reads "head hurts me". With a plural body part the verb switches to plural too: Bolą mnie nogi (my legs hurt me). English uses "I have a headache" or "my head hurts" — Polish always says "it hurts me", impersonal.

Głowa is feminine — Polish hands out grammatical gender to body parts that English just calls "the head". In Boli mnie głowa the word stays in the nominative ("who is hurting?" — the head); it is the subject of boli ("hurts"), while mnie ("me") is the accusative object. Other A1 body parts: brzuch (belly, masculine), gardło (throat, neuter), zęby (teeth, plural — verb shifts to bolą), noga (leg, feminine), ręka (hand / arm, feminine). The body part you swap in dictates whether the verb stays singular boli or jumps to plural bolą.

Woda is feminine — Polish gives gender to every noun, and water is "she". When you order it, you switch the ending: nominative woda becomes accusative wodę (whom or what would I like? — wodę). The genitive form wody pops up after quantity words: szklanka wody is "a glass of water" (a glass of what — of water). Poproszę wodę is the A1 service-standard way to ask for water at any counter.

Lekarz is a masculine ANIMATE noun — Polish splits masculine nouns into animate (people, animals) and inanimate (objects), and the animate ones get a special accusative that looks like the genitive: whom did you see? — lekarza. So "I saw the doctor" is Widziałem lekarza, not lekarz. Plural: lekarze. The feminine form for a female doctor is lekarka. False-friend warning: lekarz means "doctor", NOT "lecturer" — that is wykładowca. Note also the related word lek (medicine) from the same root: a lekarz is literally "the medicine-person".

Alergia is a feminine noun borrowed from Greek / Latin — a near-perfect cognate of English "allergy", so the vocabulary is easy; the work is in the grammar. Polish uses the "have" construction Mam alergię, just like English. The accusative ending shifts -a to -ę (whom or what do you have? — alergię). To name what you react to, add na + accusative: mam alergię na orzechy (an allergy to nuts), na gluten (to gluten), na mleko (to milk). Watch the preposition: na, not do or przeciw.

Zadzwonić is the perfective half of the verb pair dzwonić / zadzwonić. Polish marks aspect on the verb itself: the perfective views the action as one finished event (make one call now), the imperfective views it as a process or habit (codziennie dzwonię — I phone every day). Because Proszę zadzwonić asks for one specific call, the perfective is the right pick. To name what the call is for, add po + accusative: zadzwonić po pomoc (call for help), zadzwonić po lekarza (call for a doctor — the masculine animate accusative again).

Lepiej is the comparative adverb of dobrze (well, good) — exactly like English "well → better", and just as irregular. The full set is dobrze → lepiej → najlepiej (well → better → best), mirroring English good/better/best. Its opposite pair is źle → gorzej (badly → worse). Because feelings in Polish run through czuć się + adverb, "I feel better" is Czuję się lepiej — never the adjective lepszy, which would attach to a noun (lepszy dzień, a better day). You can soften or strengthen with dużo lepiej (much better) or trochę lepiej (a bit better).

Kasa is a feminine noun. It is not just the English "cash" — in Polish it covers any service window where money changes hands: a station ticket counter, a supermarket till, a theatre box office. The full ticket office is often called kasa biletowa. The base form is kasa (who is the counter?), the locative is kasie, used after w to say "at the counter" — w kasie. A synonym at the station is okienko, a diminutive of okno (window) — literally "little window".

Tam is the pointing word for "(over) there" — anywhere away from the speaker. Its partner is tu / tutaj ("here", right where the speaker is). Both are invariable — no gender, no case ending. Polish has a small set of these direction pairs: tu / tam (here / there), stąd / stamtąd (from here / from there). At a bus stop, tam signals a spot you can see but cannot reach without walking.

Odjazd is a masculine inanimate noun, so its accusative (what is leaving?) looks the same as its nominative — no ending change. The plural is odjazdy. Its partner is przyjazd (arrival) — both share the root -jazd from jechać (to go by vehicle). The question template O której jest...? Dobry is the masculine base form of the adjective for "good" — and at A1, it doubles as "right / correct" when checking a choice. Polish adjectives agree with the noun they describe: masculine dobry (dobry pociąg — right train), feminine dobra (dobra kawa — good coffee), neuter dobre (dobre piwo — good beer). In Czy to dobry pociąg? it takes the masculine ending because pociąg (train) is masculine. The related adverb is dobrze (well). A slightly more formal synonym is właściwy (the proper / fitting one).

Zamówić is the perfective half of the verb pair zamawiać / zamówić ("to order"). Polish verbs come in aspect pairs — imperfective for ongoing or repeated action, perfective for a single completed one. A taxi order is one finished action, so the perfective is natural here. The polite service template is Proszę + perfective infinitive: Proszę zamówić... ("please order..."). The accusative ending on taksówkę (whom / what do you order? — the taxi) marks it as the direct object.

Jedziemy is the 1st person plural present of jechać — "to go by vehicle". English uses one verb "to go" for everything, but Polish splits motion into two: iść (on foot — idziemy = we walk) and jechać (by car, bus, train, taxi — jedziemy = we ride). The preposition do (to/toward) takes the genitive: hotel becomes hotelu, park becomes parku. A few neuter loans like centrum stay flat (do centrum).

Zatrzymać is the perfective half of zatrzymywać / zatrzymać ("to stop"). Perfective fits because the driver does it once and it is finished. With the reflexive particle się it becomes zatrzymać się ("to come to a stop"), used when nothing is being stopped except the speaker / vehicle itself. Tutaj and tu both mean "here"; tutaj is the longer, slightly emphatic version, like "right here". Either Proszę zatrzymać tutaj or Proszę się zatrzymać tutaj is fine.

Park is a masculine inanimate noun borrowed from Western European languages — a true cognate of English "park". Its accusative looks the same as the nominative (park), but after the preposition do ("to / toward") it shifts to the genitive parku. Polish also splits motion verbs by mode: idę do parku (I am walking to the park) vs. jadę do parku (I am driving / riding there). In a city, walking is the default.

Długo is the adverb meaning "for a long time" — strictly about duration, never distance. Its partner is krótko (briefly, for a short time). Polish keeps time and space cleanly separated: ask długo / krótko about how long something takes, but daleko / blisko about how far something is. The matching adjective długi changes by gender (długi / długa / długie), but the adverb długo stays the same. The template Jak długo + verb? is the A1 way to ask "how long will X take?".

Już is a key A1 adverb meaning "already" — it marks that something has happened or that the moment has arrived (often earlier than expected). Its counterpart is jeszcze ("still / yet"). The four-way set learners need: już (already), jeszcze (still), już nie (no longer), jeszcze nie (not yet). With motion verbs, już signals arrival: Już jesteśmy (we are already here), Już idę (I am coming right now). The expression na miejscu uses the locative — miejsce shifts to miejscu after na ("at"), literally "at the spot".

Wolny is the masculine base form of the adjective. It agrees with the noun: masculine wolny (wolny pokój — free room), feminine wolna (wolna chwila — a free moment), neuter wolne (wolne miejsce — a free seat). Numer is masculine inanimate, with plural numery; the accusative looks the same as the nominative. Polish does not glue two nouns together the way English does in "room number". Instead, the specifying noun goes into the genitive: numer pokoju (literally "number of the room"). The same pattern gives you numer telefonu (phone number) and numer biletu (ticket number). Klucz is a masculine inanimate noun; its plural is klucze and its accusative looks the same as its nominative. To say "the key TO X" Polish uses the preposition do followed by the genitive: klucz do pokoju (key to the room), klucz do auta (car key) — never English-style "room key" as one compound. False-friend note for English ears: klucz sounds a little like "clue", but the two words are unrelated; this one is purely a physical key. Internet is an English loanword, treated as masculine in Polish — like most English tech borrowings with no obvious Polish gender — and almost always capitalized. At A1 it appears as a free synonym of Wi-Fi (usually written with a hyphen). Hotel staff may also ask for hasło (the password, a neuter noun) and sygnał (the signal). Łazienka is a feminine noun (Polish house-rooms tend to be feminine), and that distinctive ł — pronounced like English "w" — gives the word away. Nominative singular łazienka, plural łazienki, locative singular łazience (w łazience — in the bathroom). At A1, łazienka means the full bathroom (with a shower or bath inside). For a stand-alone toilet — at a café or restaurant — you will more often hear toaleta, and signs frequently use WC, read just like in English.

Muszę is the 1st person singular present of musieć ("must / have to") — an imperfective modal with no perfective partner. It is stronger than English "have to" and signals real necessity. Następny is the masculine citation form. Weekend is a fully naturalized English loanword in Polish — masculine, plural weekendy. It is pronounced roughly "WEE-kend" and is the everyday word; the formal native phrase koniec tygodnia ("end of the week") is rarely used in casual speech. The construction Weekend mi pasuje uses the dative pronoun mi ("to me"): Polish frames "works for me" as "is convenient TO me". The Polish week runs poniedziałek, wtorek, środa, czwartek, piątek, sobota, niedziela — sobota and niedziela together make the weekend.

Na razie is a fixed A1 farewell in the casual register — literally "for now / for the time being", open-ended and hugely popular among friends, younger speakers, and on Polish social media.
